tagline.text: Dive the Japanese ships sunk in 1944 in Coron Bay

location.label: Location
location.text: Coron Bay between Coron Island and Busuanga Island, northern Palawan (about 1 hour by boat from Coron Town)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: October–May dry season (December–March is peak season)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000 and up (for one 2-tank dive; equipment and entrance fees vary by operator)

children.text: Japanese ships sunk by a US Navy air raid on 24 September 1944 lie in Coron Bay at depths of 10–45 m. Shallow wrecks can be seen while snorkeling, and advanced divers can penetrate the deeper ones, which makes this one of the Philippines' best-known wreck diving areas.

Coron Bay is the stretch of sea between Coron Island and Busuanga Island in the Calamian Islands of northern Palawan. According to Wikipedia, most of the bay lies within the Coron Island Protected Area and is a traditional fishing ground of the indigenous Tagbanua people. The Japanese ships lie on the seabed because of an air raid on 24 September 1944. Wikipedia reports that on that day the third air group of US Navy Task Force 38 sank several Japanese vessels anchored in the bay.

The wrecks most often mentioned are the seaplane tender Akitsushima, the oil tanker Okikawa Maru, the refrigerated provision ship Irako Maru, the supply ship Kogyo Maru, the Olympia Maru (Morazán), the Taiei Maru, the Kyokuzan Maru, the Terukaze Maru and the Lusong Gunboat. Wikipedia calls the bay famous for "ten" wrecks but names only nine, so the names and the number of wrecks can differ slightly from one operator to the next. Some wrecks are also known under swapped names; sources disagree on whether the Tangat wreck is the Olympia Maru or the Taiei Maru.

Divers like these wrecks because their depths and sizes vary so much. According to Scuba Tech Philippines, the Okikawa Maru, at about 170 m long, is the largest wreck in the bay, and the deepest, the Irako Maru, is about 147 m long and lies at 34–45 m. There are also shallow wrecks such as the Lusong Gunboat, which breaks the surface and can be seen just by snorkeling, and the Terukaze Maru at 5–20 m, so companions without a diving certification can join the sightseeing too. Each wreck has its own sinking story. Scuba Tech Philippines says the Okikawa Maru was hit in the 24 September raid, burned for nearly three weeks, and sank only on 9 October 1944, while most of the others were attacked on 24 September. Wikipedia notes that engine blocks and propeller shafts from some wrecks were salvaged in the 1970s, but other equipment and some munitions remain. The Morazán's engines were also salvaged in the 1960s, so today you can see its cargo holds and boiler area.

The wrecks now serve as artificial reefs covered in coral and fish, but they are also places where the people aboard died. Citing US Navy records, Scuba Tech Philippines reports 39 deaths on the Kogyo Maru, 19 on the Morazán (Olympia Maru) including crew, gunners and passengers, and 9 on the Okikawa Maru. Some wrecks still hold ammunition, so not touching or taking anything is both basic courtesy and a safety rule. If you are new to the wrecks, plan to go from shallow to deep rather than cramming them into one day. Spend the first day getting used to wreck structure and currents on the Okikawa Maru deck or the Morazán, then move on to deeper and more complex wrecks such as the Kogyo Maru or Akitsushima the next day. The same wreck can feel very different depending on current and visibility, so leave a spare day in your schedule.

This oil tanker is about 170 m long and about 10,000 tonnes, the largest wreck in the bay. Sources give its depth as roughly 10–26 m, with the deck at about 10–16 m depending on the tide. Routes are described that enter the engine room through the propeller shaft and go on to the oil holds and crew quarters decks, and many guides recommend it as a first wreck dive. Difficulty does vary with the current, though.

blocks.title: Irako Maru: a target for deep divers

children.text: This refrigerated provision ship, built in 1937, is about 147 m long. It sank almost upright, and penetration routes are described that lead through the wheelhouse, cargo holds, galley and crew quarters. Sources put its depth anywhere from 34 to 45 m, so it is classed as a site for deep and technical divers.

This seaplane tender is about 118 m long, 4,650 tonnes, and lies at roughly 22–36 m. Fish gather around its crane and radio tower structure, and experienced divers are said to be able to enter several decks and the engine rooms. Visibility is listed at about 5–15 m, and currents are moderate to strong, so it is a demanding dive.

This supply ship is about 129 m long and lies at roughly 22–36 m (16–34 m according to some sources). You can enter the engine rooms through salvage holes, and it has six cargo holds. Hard and soft corals grow on it, and visibility is listed at 3–15 m with light to moderate current. It has tight sections, so Advanced Open Water or higher is recommended.

blocks.title: Morazán/Olympia Maru and the Tangat wreck

children.text: The Morazán (Olympia Maru), an English-built freighter-liner from 1908 that Japan is said to have seized in 1941, is about 93 m long and lies on its side at 12–25 m, which makes it relatively easy to navigate. The Tangat wreck is about 127 m long at 23–30 m, and ghost pipefish and seahorses are reported there. The names of these two wrecks differ between sources, so they are hard to pin down.

blocks.title: Lusong Gunboat and Terukaze Maru: beginner wrecks

children.text: The Lusong Gunboat lies at 5–15 m with part of it at the surface, so it counts as a snorkeling wreck, and Wikipedia describes the Terukaze Maru, at 5–20 m, as suitable for beginners. If you want to see a wreck without a diving certification, shallow sites like these are a good fit.

blocks.title: Kyokuzan Maru: a distant, deep wreck

children.text: This auxiliary freighter is about 135 m long and stands upright at 22–39 m, with army vehicles reportedly still in its cargo holds. Some guides mention visibility of 20 m or more on some days, but it takes a long boat ride to reach, so two or three dives are usually combined into one trip.

Besides the wrecks, dive operators also include Barracuda Lake (a lake with layers of cold and warm water) and Siete Pecados (a shallow coral area) in their routes. They are good places to rest between wreck dives.

items.title: One-day wreck dive (2 tanks)
items.subtitle: A shallow wreck in the morning, a mid-depth wreck in the afternoon

children.text: Board the dive operator's boat at the Coron Town pier or in front of your lodging. The wrecks in the bay are described as about
1 hour
away by boat.
For the first dive, explore a wreck with a shallow deck such as the Okikawa Maru or the Morazán. It is best to choose a time when the current is weak.
Have lunch and rest aboard the boat. The surface interval is also the time your body off-gasses nitrogen, so rest well.
For the second dive, head to a deeper, more complex wreck such as the Kogyo Maru or Akitsushima. Only divers who have completed the relevant course should enter the wreck interior.
Return to Coron Town, sort out your gear and log your dives.
The route changes with weather, current and the operator's circumstances. Discuss wreck names and order with your operator the day before.
Take a snorkeling tour boat to a wreck visible from the surface, such as the Lusong Gunboat.
Snorkel over a shallow coral area. Do not climb onto the wrecks.
Spend the afternoon combined with other tour stops (for example, Coron's lakes), then head back.

30–45 minutes
by road. It is convenient to ask your lodging in advance to arrange a van or tricycle from the airport.

items.title: By boat from El Nido or Puerto Princesa

children.text: Diving guides mention ferries from El Nido or Puerto Princesa to Coron, but note that flying is faster and more convenient. Check ferry schedules and fares locally.

children.text: The wrecks are described as about
1 hour
from Coron Town by dive operator boat.

Dive shops in Coron Town offer boat trips to wrecks and reefs. When booking, provide your certification level and last dive date, then confirm the departure point, number of dives, equipment and entry fees. The
Reggae Dive Center price list
separates certified fun diving from introductory dives for uncertified visitors.
Diving guides say the dry season from October to May has the calmest seas and best visibility. December–March is peak tourist season, so lodging and boats fill up fast; book early.
The water is warm year-round at about
, and visibility is generally reported at 10–20 m. Some wrecks list only 3–15 m, though, so it varies from day to day.

Most dive operators are concentrated in Coron Town, so staying in town makes early-morning departures easier. Ask your lodging in advance whether it has space for drying dive gear or can serve an early breakfast.
Lunch prepared by the operator is usually served aboard the boat. Tell them about allergies or dietary restrictions when you book.
For wreck diving, at least Open Water is required, and Advanced and Wreck Diver certifications are recommended; only people who have completed a separate course should enter the interior.
Deep wrecks (Irako, Akitsushima, Kyokuzan) require Advanced or higher, or deep or technical certification.
